walk.zone: Reference zone: dominant trees at their measured positions
walk.desc.emergent: It rises above the canopy: the foothill forest is a tall semi-deciduous forest with a main canopy and an emergent layer, with 40–70 tree species per hectare.
walk.desc.canopy: A tree of the main canopy of the foothill forest, a tall semi-deciduous forest with 40–70 tree species per hectare.
walk.desc.understory: A tree of the understorey, beneath the forest canopy.
walk.desc.montane: Between about 600 m and 1,200–1,400 m lies the montane forest. From 900 m, in cloud almost all year, mossy Parinari excelsa forest appears, rich in epiphytes.
walk.desc.treefern: Wet valleys of the montane forest hold tree-fern forest. Alsophila species recorded on the massif:
walk.desc.oilpalm: At Bossou, chimpanzees crack the nuts of the oil palm with a stone hammer and anvil.
walk.desc.raphia: A raphia palm recorded on the massif; placed here by the water.
walk.desc.protea: The transition from forest to high-altitude grassland passes through Protea bushland.
walk.desc.savanna: The massif is surrounded by savanna, cleared by fire for farming and livestock.
walk.desc.regrowth: Here the land-cover map shows trees but the canopy-height model measures under 6 m: probably regrowth, fallow or farm bush.

walk.site.title: Nut-cracking stones
walk.site.note: Illustrative site: its location is not real.
walk.person.title: Villager – fictional figure
walk.person.note: A generic, fictional figure: no real person is shown. The activity follows the sources below; the spot is illustrative.
walk.act.pound: Pounding in a mortar. In Forest Guinea, boiled palm fruit is pounded in mortars, then kneaded to extract the oil.
walk.act.carry: Carrying water or a load. In Guinea, children fetch water and firewood and help prepare food.
walk.act.firewood: Bringing firewood. In Guinea, children fetch water and firewood and help prepare food.
walk.act.baby: Mothers carry their babies on their backs, tied in a wrapper.
walk.act.hoe: Working in a field. At Bossou, upland rice and cassava are the staples; among the Kpelle, men clear the fields and women plant.
walk.act.sit: Talking in the shade in front of a house (everyday scene, no specific source).
walk.act.walk: On the way along a real path (OpenStreetMap) linking houses, fields and villages.
walk.act.play: Children playing (everyday scene, no specific source).
walk.village.bossou: Bossou: about 2,000 people (village), Manon. Upland rice, cassava, oil palm; market on Wednesdays. Chimpanzees are protected there by a taboo.
walk.house.roundText: The region's traditional house is round, wattle-and-daub, under a conical thatched roof; it now predominates only in remote villages.
walk.house.rectText: Newer houses are mostly rectangular, wattle-and-daub or block, roofed with corrugated metal, often with a porch.
walk.house.note: Position and size: a building mapped in OpenStreetMap. Shape and materials: typical of the region, not surveyed house by house.
walk.area.industrialText: Ground mapped as industrial, quarry or brownfield in OpenStreetMap.
walk.area.mineNote: Outline: OpenStreetMap. The benches and bare ground are a reconstruction from this outline and the terrain, not a survey.
walk.area.fieldText: At Bossou, upland rice and cassava are the staples; maize, banana, pineapple and fruit are also grown.
walk.area.rockText: Here the land-cover map or OpenStreetMap shows rock or bare ground without vegetation.
walk.area.wetlandText: Waterlogged ground covered with tall grasses and marsh plants.

museum.relief.title: The massif in relief
museum.relief.short: The 31 × 31 km around the ridge, built from satellite elevation data, with the relief exaggerated twice so it reads clearly. The numbered markers point to the exhibits in this gallery.
museum.relief.long: The model is computed from the Copernicus DEM elevation model (one height about every 30 m). The colours come from the ESA WorldCover land-cover map: forest in dark green, grassland and savanna in ochre, cropland in light beige. The amber line follows the reserve boundary (WDPA, simplified); the light dashes are the national borders (approximate). The fine lines are 200 m contour lines.
museum.window.title: The view from the summit
museum.window.short: What you would see from Mount Richard-Molard: a computer-generated image calculated from the real terrain and land cover. It is not a photograph.
museum.window.long: The view was rendered with Blender (Cycles engine) from the same terrain model and land-cover map as the relief model. The plants are generic free models (Poly Haven, CC0), not Nimba species. For real photographs of the summit, see exhibit 1.
